title: Propositional Logic
description: Propositional logic is the logic of whole statements joined by connectives: and, or, not, if-then, if-and-only-if. Its semantics are given by truth tables, which decide every formula mechanically — propositional logic is decidable. It underlies digital circuit design (gates are truth functions) and the boolean conditions in every program.
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Predicate (First-Order) Logic
description: First-order logic adds quantifiers ('for all', 'there exists') and predicates over objects, letting it express 'all humans are mortal' formally. It is the standard logic of mathematics: Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory is written in it. Gödel's completeness theorem says every valid first-order argument has a proof, while his incompleteness theorems bound what any consistent system can prove about arithmetic.
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Informal Logic and Argumentation
description: Informal logic studies real-world reasoning: identifying premises and conclusions, mapping argument structure, and spotting fallacies like ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, and appeal to authority. It is the logic of essays, debates, law, and journalism. Its central skill is charity — reconstructing the strongest version of an argument before evaluating it.
demo:
fallacies = ['ad hominem', 'straw man', 'false dilemma', 'appeal to authority', 'begging the question']
print('spot the fallacy; then steelman the argument before judging it')
print('fallacy watchlist:', ', '.join(fallacies))
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Symbolic Logic
description: Symbolic logic is the program — begun by Frege, Russell, and Whitehead — of expressing reasoning in a precise formal notation with explicit inference rules like modus ponens. It turned logic from a philosophical art into a mathematical science and made computers possible: every programming language's semantics rests on it. Natural deduction and sequent calculi are its standard proof systems.
demo:
print('modus ponens: from P and (P -> Q), infer Q')
print('modus tollens: from (P -> Q) and ~Q, infer ~P')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Modal Logic
description: Modal logic adds the operators 'necessarily' and 'possibly' to reason about necessity, possibility, knowledge, and obligation. Kripke's possible-worlds semantics (1960s) made it rigorous: 'necessarily P' means P holds in all accessible worlds. It formalizes philosophical arguments, program verification (dynamic logic), and AI reasoning about belief.
demo:
print('necessarily P: P holds in ALL accessible possible worlds')
print('possibly P: P holds in SOME accessible possible world')
print('Kripke semantics made modal logic rigorous (1960s)')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Temporal Logic
description: Temporal logic reasons about time with operators like 'always,' 'eventually,' 'next,' and 'until.' Linear temporal logic (LTL) and computation tree logic (CTL) are the workhorses of hardware and software model checking — verifying that a chip or protocol always behaves correctly. Amir Pnueli's work on temporal logic won the 1996 Turing Award.
demo:
print('G(request -> F grant): every request is eventually granted')
print('LTL/CTL power hardware & software model checking')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Fuzzy Logic
description: Fuzzy logic (Zadeh, 1965) allows truth values between 0 and 1, modeling vagueness: 'the room is warm' can be 0.7 true. Fuzzy controllers drive washing machines, subway brakes, and cameras, using rules like 'if temperature is high and rising fast, then cooling is strong.' It trades classical bivalence for engineering practicality with graded concepts.
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Paraconsistent Logic
description: Paraconsistent logics tolerate contradictions without explosion — in classical logic, one contradiction entails everything (ex falso quodlibet), but paraconsistent systems quarantine the inconsistency so reasoning can continue. They model inconsistent databases, legal codes with conflicting statutes, and dialetheist philosophies that accept some true contradictions. Relevance logic is a close cousin with similar motivations.
demo:
print('classical: P and ~P entails EVERYTHING (explosion)')
print('paraconsistent: quarantine the contradiction, keep reasoning')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Intuitionistic Logic
description: Intuitionistic logic (Brouwer, Heyting) rejects the law of excluded middle: a statement is true only when there is a constructive proof of it. 'P or not P' is not a theorem without a construction deciding which. It matches computation exactly — the Curry-Howard correspondence identifies intuitionistic proofs with programs, making it the logic of type theory and proof assistants.
demo:
print('intuitionistic: P is true only with a constructive proof')
print('Curry-Howard: proofs ARE programs; the logic of type theory')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Deontic Logic
description: Deontic logic formalizes obligation, permission, and prohibition — the logic of norms, laws, and contracts. Its operators ('it ought to be that...') model legal reasoning and the rules governing autonomous agents. Famous puzzles like the contrary-to-duty paradox ('you ought not steal; if you steal, do it quietly') drove refinements that matter for machine ethics and compliance systems.
demo:
print('O(p): it ought to be that p | P(p): p is permitted')
print('models: laws, contracts, duties of autonomous agents')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Epistemic Logic
description: Epistemic logic reasons about knowledge with operators like 'agent A knows that P,' using possible-worlds semantics where worlds are indistinguishable to the agent. It solves puzzles like the muddy children and the sum-and-product, and it models distributed systems — what each process knows determines what protocols can achieve. Common knowledge ('everyone knows that everyone knows...') is its deepest concept.
demo:
print('K_a(P): agent a knows P (P holds in all worlds a cannot rule out)')
print('common knowledge drives distributed protocols')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Higher-Order Logic
description: Higher-order logic allows quantification over predicates and functions themselves, not just objects — expressing 'for all properties P...' directly. It is more expressive than first-order logic but loses completeness and compactness: there is no complete proof system for full second-order semantics. Proof assistants like HOL and Isabelle are built on it, trading decidability for expressive power.
demo:
print('second-order: quantify over properties, not just objects')
print('expressive, but no complete proof system (full semantics)')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Many-Valued Logic
description: Many-valued logics use more than two truth values: Kleene's three-valued logic adds 'undefined' for partial computation, and Łukasiewicz's extends truth across the whole [0,1] interval. They model undefined expressions, future contingents (Aristotle's sea battle), and gradual truth. Fuzzy logic is the most applied member of this family.
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Relevance Logic
description: Relevance logics require premises to be genuinely relevant to conclusions, rejecting classical oddities like 'if the moon is cheese then 2+2=4' counting as valid. They block the paradoxes of material implication by demanding variable sharing between antecedent and consequent. Developed by Anderson and Belnap, they formalize the intuition that valid reasoning must connect its parts.
demo:
print('rejects: (P and ~P) -> Q and P -> (Q -> P) as valid')
print('demand: antecedent and consequent must share content')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.

title: Quantum Logic
description: Quantum logic (Birkhoff and von Neumann, 1936) rebuilds propositional structure on the lattice of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space, where the distributive law fails — reflecting that quantum measurements disturb each other. It asks what logic looks like when observation changes the observed. It remains more a research program than an engineering tool, but it illuminates the strangeness of quantum reasoning.
demo:
print('Birkhoff-von Neumann 1936: propositions = subspaces of Hilbert space')
print('distributive law fails: measurement disturbs the measured')
provenance: Public reference: standard logic references (Aristotelian canon, Frege/Russell/Whitehead, modern modal and non-classical logic texts); verified 2026-10-21.
